sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive approaches with large language models, such as long chain-of-thought reasoning, have become the default for new AI applications because they reach higher accuracy on a wide range of tasks. In production, however, they give inconsistent answers, require parsing of outputs, and add cost and latency. Decision models address this: given a question and a set of options supplied by the user, they return a probability distribution over the options without autoregressive decoding. We present Drex, a family of four open decision models with 8B (DLM), 9B (v1.5), 35B with 3B active (v2.0), and 27B (Max) parameters. Each request consists of a state (a document, record, or agent context, optionally with images) and questions about it, each asking for a choice among options, a yes/no judgment, or a score on an ordered scale. Training combines supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF), plus vision tuning for Max. Ablations show that RLAF improves accuracy and that consistency losses improve robustness to option order. On Decision Index 0.4.1, Max sets a new state of the art among the decision models we compare (67.52 on the public suite vs. 60.70 for Jev 1.14.0). On Decision Bench v4, it is statistically tied with d3-turbo and GPT-6 Sol and trails Claude Opus 5.5 by 1.6 points, and it has the highest accuracy among decision models on DecideBench. Max answers a typical request in 183 ms, against about 2.0 s for GPT-6 Sol and 3.5 s for Claude Opus 5.5, and its outputs are stable under option reordering. All four models are open source: https://github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Language models learn their representations through single objective: predicting the next token in sequence, or, in the case of masked language models, predicting tokens withheld from their context [8, 13]. These representations, however, transfer to many tasks in which no text is generated. Such tasks can often be categorized into one of three kinds: Classification maps an input to one label from fixed set [13, 58]. Scoring maps an input to number, such as the relevance of passage to query [34, 46] or the similarity of two sentences [59]. Embedding maps an input to vector that is compared, clustered or searched [5, 59, 73]. When utilizing autoregressive models to solve these kinds of tasks, the same design question always arises: How to read the answer from model whose native output is distribution over each token? To address this, three solutions have been proposed. Encoder models are fine-tuned with small head at the last layera linear layer to produce single score or additionally softmax over fixed set of output labels [13, 46]. T5 recast these tasks as text-to-text, with the label generated as string [58], and for decoder-only models, prompting for generated label became common interface [8]. Recent work fine-tunes decoder-only models to return scores and embeddings directly [5, 34, 73]. In all three of the above solutions, the shape of the output is fixed before the model is deployed. classification head has its labels fixed at training time, reranker returns one number per candidate, an embedding model returns one vector per input. In contrast, we are interested in the setting where the set of candidate outputs changes across inputs: the user supplies context, question and the set of candidate outputs, and the model produces one probability per option. fixed head does not suffice in this setting. One route is to prompt an autoregressive model for the answer and parse the output text; another is to generate the option and constrain the generation to the allowed strings, technique with long history in sequence generation [2, 25, 65, 75]. The second option guarantees valid output, and the probability of an option is computed as the product of per-token probabilities, but such model is not trained to predict distribution over set of options. Additionally, computing the output probabilities of constrained generation involves renormalizing the per-token probabilities at every step, and the result can differ from the distribution that the model would assign to the valid options as whole strings, for example when options share prefixes or differ in length [51]. Scoring every option separately and renormalizing across options recovers distribution over the valid options, but at the cost of one forward pass per option. Specialized models that return probability rather than generated text have been built for single, domain-specific decisions, such as predicting whether sales conversation will convert [33], but their output is fixed to that one decision. In contrast, our approach is to develop new kind of readout: one that performs classification in which the set of options is given at inference time, by the user. We use the term decision model to refer to model

Pointer models (e.g., Drex DLM, v1.5, v2.0) are decision models where the context is encoded once and then shared across multiple questions, reducing cost and latency in appropriate applications. Drex Max re-encodes the context for each question using dense multimodal backbone with non-causal full attention, and reads the answer from readout head: each option is labeled with single-token code (A, B, . . . ), and bias-free linear layer maps the final hidden state to one logit per code, up to 255 codes (Section 5.2). This results in higher accuracy in exchange for increased cost per question. In developing these models, we aim to resolve the question: Can single model serve arbitrary option sets with calibrated probabilities, answer many questions over one long context, maintain stability when the options are reordered, and do so at production latency? In this report, we investigate the above question by considering the design choices in the development of decision models and their effect on the models behavior and performance. We organize this investigation into four research questions: RQ1 Calibration. How well do the probabilities returned by decision models match their empirical accuracy, overall and across application areas and numbers of options? Does single global temperature, fit on held-out decisions, improve this calibration? RQ2 Option order. How sensitive are the probabilities and decisions of pointer and readout-head models to the order in which the options are presented? RQ3 Training. How much does each stage of the training pipeline contribute to the final model: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with consistency losses, reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards adjusted by the output probabilities of an LRM-as-a-judge under KL penalty relative to the SFT model (RLAF), and vision SFT? Does the vision stage preserve accuracy on text inputs? RQ4 Capacity, attention, and modality. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using dense multimodal backbone and bidirectional attention versus shared-state pointer head? We study these questions by training and studying four models that share one interface (Section 3) and common training-data base (Section 6.1), which we extend for training Drex Max. Most of the evidence is comparative, across models, training stages, and inference-time interventions. Therefore, outside one ablation of Drex Maxs training (Section 8.8), we report associations and trade-offs rather than causal relationships; Section 10 lists the comparisons we did not run, and the hypotheses that require further experimentation, such as which specific changes in the design and training of Max drive its gains. The pointer models are built on top of the open Kev code base. We evaluate the following properties, which are desirable for decision models: accuracy, as compared against frontier and other decision-specialized models via paired statistical comparisons; calibration, measured on hundreds of thousands of decisions that span diverse applications; robustness to the order of options; and accuracy on image inputs, where we compare the models performance when given image inputs versus equivalent text inputs. We additionally measure the contribution of each training stage to these properties. We quantify robustness to the order of options with the flip rate, which is the fraction of decisions for which the option with the highest probability changes when the order of the options changes. We quantify the usefulness of models confidence with selective accuracy, which is the accuracy of the model on the fraction of decisions on which it is most confident. Contributions. Calibration at scale (RQ1). We measure the calibration of Drex Max, v2.0, v1.5, and commercial baseline on about 230k decisions each. We report bootstrap confidence intervals; breakdowns by domain and by the number of options; selective accuracy; and the effect of using single temperature parameter fitted on held-out data (Section 8.4). We find that the top option changes with the order mostly on decisions that have many options and low model confidence. On these workloads, declining to answer the decisions on which the top option changes with the order is no more accurate than declining to answer the decisions with the lowest confidence. Averaging the three probability distributions predicted by the model for the respective three orders improves log loss but not accuracy (Section 8.5). training recipe for highly capable decision models (RQ3). We provide three-stage recipe, which we use to train Drex Max (Section 6). The first stage is supervised fine-tuning (SFT). The second stage is reinforcement learning from adjusted feedback (RLAF). The third stage is SFT of the image encoder and of its projection into the language model, which teaches the model to make decisions from images. During the first stage, we add two consistency terms to the SFT loss since the architecture of Drex Max does not make its answers independent of the order of the options. The first term penalizes change in the predicted distribution when the options are permuted; the second term penalizes change when the sentences or fields of the state are shuffled (Section 6.2). During RLAF, the model is optimized to maximize reward that combines the verified correct answer with the probabilities that judge model assigns to the options. The objective is regularized by the KL divergence between the output distribution of the current model and that of its own SFT checkpoint. Section 6.5 derives the gradient of this objective and the closed-form output distribution that maximizes it. An ablation of the training of Drex Max on its own backbone and training data  (Table 7)  shows that RLAF improves the Decision Index score by 2.0 points, that the addition of the consistency terms in the loss function lowers the flip rate from 6.3% to 4.2%, and that the third stage does not reduce accuracy on text inputs. seven-checkpoint analysis of the training of Drex v2.0 shows the relative contribution of each step in the training recipe of the pointer models (Section 8.7). Drex Max (RQ4). We present Drex Max, dense (i.e., not mixture-of-experts) multimodal decision model trained from Qwen3.8-27B. The model removes the causal attention mask in its full-attention layers, and it produces its answer with readout head, i.e., bias-free linear layer that maps the final hidden state to vector of 255 logits, one per option code (Section 5). We describe the cost of running the model, which is higher per question than that of the pointer models since the model re-encodes the context for every question (Section D.1). We also measure how the accuracy of the model on decisions that involve images changes when it receives the image itself rather than text description and transcription of the image (Section 8.2). One interface on four backbones. We develop single interface that seamlessly functions with four distinct backbone models. The pointer head is added to the last layer of each of the following backbone models: (1) Gated DeltaNet hybrid model, (2) diffusion language model with bidirectional attention over the context, and (3) sparse mixture-of-experts model. The readout head is added to the last layer of dense multimodal model with 27 billion parameters. All four models, one per backbone, accept the same requests and return the same output format (Section 3), and we compare them in Section E. Paired evaluation. We evaluate the models on Decision Index (versions 0.2.1 and 0.4.1, and version 0.4.1 with its private tests), Decision Bench v4 (with images given as input in image encoder and as text), JevBench, DecideBench, game arena, computer-use judging probe, and vision suite, and we compare them with frontier chat models on the same samples. We report per-benchmark tables, Wilson intervals for accuracies, paired bootstrap intervals for differences between models, and exact McNemar tests throughout (Section 8). Deployment and inference optimization. We describe how our decision models are deployed and the techniques we leverage to improve inference speed (Section 9). Release status. All four models are released as open-weight models; the weights and inference code are collected at github.com/nace-ai/drex-decision-models. sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Decision models draw on several lines of work: likelihood scoring and multiple-choice prompting with fixed set of candidate answers [8, 61], cross-encoders and pointer networks [46, 71], the option-order sensitivity of language models [53, 85], and calibration and proper scoring rules [21, 23]. The four Drex models are each built on different language-model architectures: diffusion language model [19], Gated DeltaNet hybrid model [56, 78, 79, 82, 83], and sparse mixture of experts language model (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B) [18, 27, 55, 64]. In hybrid models, such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, some layers utilize global attention while others utilize linear attention. The training methodology of Drex Max includes an RLAF training stage, which is an instance of KL-regularized learning from feedback [49, 57]. The main benchmarks are Decision Index [37] and Decision Bench [4]. Section discusses each line of work in detail. Relation to Jev and Kev. The interface follows Jevs System One API; the pointer models are built on the open Kev code base [50], and Drex Maxs attention pattern and readout adopt the open pplx-decider design [52], but we trained its weights ourselves, starting from the Qwen3.8-27B base model. Drex inherits number of features from Kev: the packed encoding with block-causal mask (Section 4), the encoding of each question as separate causal sequence that is conditioned on cached state, the pointer head over tokens that delimit each option, and the loss functions for training (cross-entropy, squared Cramér distance, permutation consistency). To the best of our knowledge, everything else is novel, especially in their application to decision models: the additional training stage from adjusted feedback (Section 6.3), the training of the readout head of Drex Max (Section 6), the training of its image encoder and the projection of that encoder into the language model (Section 5.3), the evaluation (Section 8), and the inference stack (Section 9).

sections.content: Desirable properties. The following are desirable properties for decision models: Closed-world output: The distribution pk is supported on Ok, because the output of the model is defined only over the supplied options. It is not supported on Ok merely because the input instructs the model to choose among the options (i.e., prompting) or because generated text is restricted to the options (i.e., constrained decoding). Question independence: The distribution pk does not depend on which other questions are asked in the same request. Therefore, question receives the same probabilities, up to floating-point error, whether it is queried alone, processed together with other questions in one batch, or replayed later from cached request. Order robustness: The predicted probability of an option is invariant with respect to the ordering of the options in the input. That is, for any permutation π of Ok, pk( πOk) = π pk( Ok). weaker version of this condition is that the top option is unchanged under every permutation. Calibration: Pr[arg maxj pk,j is correct maxj pk,j = c] = c. This property is desirable, for example, because threshold on the confidence can then serve as rule for routing decisions. Grounding in every modality supplied: When the evidence is an image, the model must process the image and incorporate the information therein when forming its prediction, instead of relying on text description of the image. The architectures of all Drex models guarantee the first two properties by construction (Section C). The last three properties are learned, so we measure how well each of these properties holds rather than assuming that they hold. We measure the expected calibration error over 15 equal-width bins (ECE). We also measure the log loss (also, negative log-likelihood, abbreviated NLL), the Brier score, and selective accuracy, which is the accuracy on the fraction of decisions with the highest confidence (Section in the Appendix). We measure order robustness with the top-1 flip rate, which is the fraction of decisions whose top option changes under permutation of the options (Section in the Appendix).

sections.title: 4 Pointer architecture
sections.content: Every Drex pointer model is pretrained language-model backbone fθ plus pointer head (Wq, Wk) (Figure 1). Nothing is decoded at inference time. Drex Max uses different output head and attention pattern and is described in Section 5. Packing and attention. request is serialized, or packed, into one token sequence that consists of state segment followed by one question block per question. Each question block is contiguous block of text that contains the instruction, the options, and final <decide> token, in this order; each option is enclosed between an opening tag <opt> and closing tag </opt>. These tags and the other delimiters are special tokens, which do not appear in the text supplied by the user (Eq. (16)). On attention-only backbones, the sequence is encoded under block-causal mask (Figure 10, Appendix Eq. (17)): every token of question block can attend to all tokens of the state and to the preceding tokens of the same question block, but not to any token of another question block. Drex DLM adds bidirectional attention within the state, so that each token in the state can attend to every other token in the state, including later ones. Drex v1.5 and v2.0 use hybrid models as backbones, which interleave layers with linear attention (Gated DeltaNet layers) with global attention layers. Hybrid models cannot apply an arbitrary attention mask; for these models, each question is processed as separate causal sequence that consists of the state followed by that questions block, and the encoding of the state is cached and reused across questions. Hence, up to floating-point error, pk depends only on the state and question (Section C). Adding, removing, or reordering the other questions of request therefore does not change pk, because the position IDs of the question blocks are set such that, in terms of the position IDs, each question block immediately follows the end of the state. sections.title: 5 Drex Max: a dense multimodal decision model
sections.content: The pointer models answer question by comparing hidden states inside one causal encoding of the context. Drex Max asks different question of the architecture: what is the effect on the accuracy and the inference cost of the resulting decision model if every question can attend to the entire request in both directions, and the backbone is dense 27B model with an image encoder? The attention pattern and output head of Drex Max follow the design of the publicly released pplx-decider model [52]. This section describes the architecture; we train its weights from the Qwen3.8-27B base model with the recipe of Section D.

The notation γj: ok,j means that the text of option is written after its option code γj and colon, for example A: refund request. The option codes γ1, . . . , γ255 = A, . . . , Z, AA, . . . are each single token in the vocabulary, and <ans> is fixed special token that ends the sequence; the answer is read from the hidden state at its position. Let hk Rd be the final-layer hidden state at the last position of xk. The readout head is bias-free linear layer Wr R255d that maps hk to vector of 255 logits, one for each option code; only the first Kk logits, which belong to the Kk options of the question, are kept: (4) zk = Wrhk R255, pk,j = exp(zk,j/T ) i=1 exp(zk,i/T ) (cid:80)Kk , = 1, . . . , Kk, (5) where > 0 is the temperature parameter. We set =1.009, value fitted on held-out records after the last training stage (Section D); it is close to 1, so it changes the probabilities only slightly, and it does not change the most probable option. The readout head has 255 5,120 1.3M parameters, comparable to the pointer head. The output format described in Section 3 is unchanged: pk is supported on Ok by construction, 255, and the confidence statistics of Eq. (1) are computed from pk in the same way. Comparison with the pointer head. The two heads differ in how they represent each option. In the pointer head, option is represented by its own hidden state hok,j , which summarizes the text of the option, and the score of the option is computed from this hidden state. In the readout head, option is identified only by the code γj that precedes it, so the backbone must learn to associate each code with the text of its option, which is the symbol-binding problem of multiple-choice prompting [61], and permutation of the options changes which of the 255 logits corresponds to which option. Order robustness is therefore entirely learned in Drex Max, which is why we measure it directly (Section 8.5). In exchange, the readout head lets the full-attention layers compare all options with one another and with the context in both directions before the answer is computed, which the causal pointer cannot.

sections.title: 5.3 Images
sections.content: Drex Max keeps the image encoder of the backbone, the part of the model that converts images into token embeddings. Each image in is split into patches, encoded by the vision transformer [16], and merged into visual tokens that enter the sequence ahead of the state (Eq. (4)), as in the standard encoder-plus-LM layout [32]. Because each question is encoded as distinct sequence containing the images of the request, every question in request can attend to all of the images in that request. request can contain both questions that depend on the images and questions that do not. Video is handled by sampling frames and passing them as images, since the model has no temporal encoder. Cost. Because the full-attention layers are non-causal, the representation of the state depends on the question, so it cannot be cached across questions (Section D.1): Drex Max pays for the state once per question, the pointer models once per request. For short contexts the difference is small: at launch, the median latency of single request was 183 ms for Drex Max, against 151 ms for Drex v2.0 and 145 ms for Drex v1.5 (see Table 8, which describes how latency was measured). For many questions over long documents, the pointer models remain the cheaper choice.

sections.title: 6.4 Specialization stages
sections.content: For some task families on which the model remains weak after supervised fine-tuning, we perform an additional stage of training, which we call specialization stage. It is performed after supervised fine-tuning and before RLAF, and continues training from the final SFT checkpoint, resulting in model that is specialized for the task family of interest. Each specialization stage targets single task family; and we sometimes apply multiple specialization stages to model, in sequence, with the aim of each stage being to improve the models performance in one task family. However, among the released models, the specialization stage is only used in the training of Drex v2.0 (Section 8.7). The specialization stage is not used in the training of Drex v1.5 and Drex Max. The specialization stage trains low-rank adapters [26] rather than all weights. Its training data consist of: (1) decisions in the target task family whose correct answers are computed by solver, (2) difficult examples from that family which are mined from existing data, and (3) replayed examples from earlier training stages, which prevent the model from forgetting other tasks. For the same purpose, we add KL penalty KL(pref pθ) to the loss, where pref is the distribution predicted by the checkpoint at the start of this training stage; this term penalizes divergence from that checkpoint. The final checkpoint is selected on held-out split of the stages own training data, not on any benchmark. Contamination filtering. No evaluation example from Decision Index or JevBench is used for training, and we drop training records whose state exactly matches, or shares more than two 8-word sequences with, any benchmark example. These filters miss two kinds of contamination: paraphrased benchmark items, and knowledge of benchmarks that may be distilled from teacher models that were themselves trained on benchmark data.

sections.title: 7 Experimental setup
sections.content: Decision Index. The Decision Index is recognized public leaderboard consisting of set of decision benchmarks, with each benchmark being categorized into one of 5 domains (i.e., areas) [37]. For each benchmark, we convert the official metric (e.g., accuracy, macro-F1, nDCG, Brier skill, . . . ) into chance-corrected skill metric, where 0 is uniform guessing and 100 is perfect, so that binary task and 150-option task are comparable (Section P). In our results, we report the non-corrected metric as raw, and unanswered or unsupported requests count as wrong. Versions of the Decision Index differ in their set of decision benchmarks and the weight of each benchmark in the set (Section G). The Decision Index validation set is partitioned into two subsets: the public subset and private subset, which is hidden. The private subset is further subdivided into same-skill subset, which contains examples for tasks that are similar to those in the public subset, and new-domain subset, which contains examples for domains that do not exist in the public subset. Two scores can be reported on Decision Index: (1) public-only score which is measured using examples from the subset, and (2)

sections.title: DREX TECHNICAL REPORT
sections.content: a full score which is computed using formula that depends on the models performance on both the public and private subsets. In our experiments, we compute the public scores and we submit our models to the maintainers of Decision Index to compute the full score. Our evaluations of Drex Max, v2.0, v1.5, and GPT-6 Luna Decisions on Decision Index 0.4.1 each cover all 140,620 requests from the public subset (140,178 of which were not discarded by the Decision Index maintainers), where we record all per-request predicted probabilities. Decision Bench v4. Decision Bench v4 is benchmark with 1,071 single-question decisions across 35 tasks in 11 professional categories, sampled from 36 public datasets of real records [4]; 949 are text-only, 62 combine text and an image, and 60 are image questions. Every question with an image also comes with text rendering of the image (a description and, where applicable, text extracted via OCR). We evaluate Drex Max twice: once with only the text rendering of each image, and once with the image itself provided to the model through its image encoder. All other decision models receive the text rendering; GPT-6 Sol, Claude Opus 5.5, and d3-turbo, which is commercial decision model, additionally receive the images whenever available. Native probabilities are available for every decision model, so we report the expected calibration error (ECE) and the log loss for them; chat models return verbalized probabilities, which we do not score for calibration. Other evaluations. We also evaluate on JevBench-231 [67], DecideBench v1.1 [84], an OpenSpiel game arena [31], an OSWorld judging probe [81], the Decision Index vision suites [37], and longcontext documents (Section G). Baselines. We compare against handful of baseline systems.The decision-specialized systems are Jev 1.13.0 [1] and 1.14.0 [70], GPT-6 Luna Decisions [47], d3-turbo [72], and other models with published entries on the Decision Index leaderboard. We also compare against two frontier chat models, GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, which we prompt with lettered options and ask for JSON-formatted probabilities. Leaderboard numbers are taken from the official leaderboards [37]; all other quantities reported in Section 8 come from our own experiments unless otherwise marked as reported. Whenever model card reports separate run on the same benchmark, we report only the accuracy that we measured. For accuracy on fixed set of questions, such as Decision Bench v4 and JevBench-231, we report 95% Wilson confidence intervals [77]. When we compare two models on the same questions, we use two methods: First, we compute percentile bootstrap over questions (5,000 resamples) which gives confidence interval on the difference in accuracy of the two models. Second, the exact two-sided McNemar test determines whether the two models are equally accurate, using only the questions on which exactly one of the two models answers correctly [14, 17, 35]. On the Decision Index, request can contain several decisions about the same state, and these decisions are correlated, so we resample whole requests rather than decisions. For the confidence interval on the Decision Index score itself, we resample benchmarks within each domain. This interval shows how much the score would change if different set of benchmarks had been chosen, rather than if different set of questions were sampled within each benchmark. We run many statistical tests in this paper and do not adjust their p-values for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni adjustments). An isolated p-value near 0.05 should therefore be interpreted as suggestive, not conclusive.

Thus, we recommend that, for any application of Drex Max that contains component that depends on whether Maxs predicted probability exceeds threshold, and that serves narrow type of request, the temperature parameter should be tuned on labeled decisions of that type. Because every output is normalized distribution over the supplied options, the models predicted probability in each decision can be read directly from its output. An application can therefore flag the low-confidence decisions of decision model for human review without training separate model to predict which decisions are likely to be wrong. The request together with the predicted distribution serves as the audit record of each decision. Keeping only the 80% of decisions on which Drex Max is most confident raises its precision from 87.9% (precision@top-100%, i.e., accuracy on all decisions) to 96.1% (precision@top-80%), and keeping the most confident 50% raises it further to 99.3% (precision@top-50%; Figure 7b). sections.title: 8.5 Option-order robustness
sections.content: Protocol. We drew sample of requests from the 37 benchmarks of the public index of Decision Index 0.4.1, stratified by benchmark: we sampled from each benchmark separately, so that no benchmark contributes more than 40 requests. From each benchmark, we kept only the requests in which every question is choice question with at least one gold label that is string, the state has at most 12,000 characters, and there are at most 16 questions. We then shuffled these requests with fixed random seed and took the first 40 (or all of them, if the benchmark has fewer), which gives 1,175 requests (Section L). We gave each request to four models, Drex Max, Drex v2.0, Drex v1.5, and Jev 1.14.0, through public APIs. Each request was given three times: with the original ordering of the options, with the reversed ordering, and with random permutation of the options of every question. Of the 1,175 sampled requests, 1,040 were answered by all four models under all three orderings. We excluded the remaining requests for every model, for one of two reasons. First, in some requests, the options are structured objects with several fields rather than strings (for example, musical chord or preference profile), and the public APIs reject such requests because they fail the schema validation of the API. The evaluation code of the Decision Index converts these options into strings before it passes them to model, but we gave the requests to the APIs unchanged. Second, some requests were rejected by the Jev API. This leaves 1,591 decisions (915 binary, 503 with 35 options, 173 with six or more). Before we compare the outputs of model under two orderings, we map the probabilities that it returns for reordered request back to the original ordering of the options. Metrics. Flip rate and accuracy. We find that random permutations of the option set change the most probable option in 4.3% of Drex Maxs decisions, 5.9% of v2.0s, 5.3% of v1.5s, and 4.3% of Jevs (Table 5, Figure 8). Reversing the option set, which moves every option, has greater effect on the output of every model (5.78.4%). Despite its readout head, whose logits are tied to positions (Section 5.2), Drex Max is as stable as Jev and more stable than the pointer models, whose hybrid backbones cannot isolate options. Accuracy, however, changes little; Max scores 83.6% under the original ordering and 83.4% under the permutation, and the flips are nearly balanced between gains and losses. Order instability and confidence. Decisions for which the most probable option changes across the three orderings are far less accurate than those that do not: 37.6% vs. 87.2% for Drex Max, and 37.746.8% vs. 81.884.7% for the other models (Table 20 in the Appendix). Order instability is thus strong signal that decision is wrong. Since Drex can be used in applications where it should produce abstentions for some decisions, we compare two rules for determining when to abstain. The first rule abstains on the decisions that are unstable under reordering (i.e., decisions for which the

sections.title: DREX TECHNICAL REPORT
sections.content: most probable option is different under each of the three orderings), and the second rule abstains on the decisions with the lowest confidence where is the number of abstentions produced by the first rule. Both rules yield almost the same accuracy on the non-abstention decisions: 87.2% vs. 87.1% for Max, and for every model, the two accuracies differ by at most 0.4 percentage points (Table 20 in the Appendix). We also define the coverage of rule as the fraction of decisions on which it does not abstain. At coverage of 8085%, abstaining on the decisions that are either unstable under reordering or have low confidence raises accuracy by at most 0.6 percentage points over abstaining on low confidence alone. In this sample, the decisions that are changed by option reordering are largely those to which the model already assigns low confidence, so user who scrutinizes the models output confidence gains little from further scrutiny of the models sensitivity to option reordering. This observation is an association, not causal account of every flip, and the set of decisions with six or more options, which has the highest flip rate, contains only 173 decisions. Further experiments to replicate this result on larger, independent workloads would be valuable. We also consider an ensemble of orderings, which averages the three probability distributions that the model returns for decision, option by option, and predicts the option with the highest average probability. The ensemble of the three orderings  (Table 5)  changes accuracy by at most 0.8 percentage points but lowers log loss for every model, and significantly so for Max (a reduction of 0.014 nats, 95% confidence interval [0.005, 0.024]) and Jev (a reduction of 0.044 nats, 95% confidence interval [0.018, 0.075]), and lowers ECE for three of the four models. Option count. Binary decisions almost never flip (1.0% for Max, 2.0% for the others), but with six or more options, 1316% of decisions change under permutation for every model, including Jev. These are the decisions to which the model already assigns low confidence (Table 19 in the Appendix), so most flips change the top option among options with nearly equal probabilities. The practical consequence for user is the same as for the small numerical differences in the output probabilities that arise at inference time when request is processed in different batch (Section 9.2). If the confidence of decision on question with many options is close to some behaviorally-significant threshold, the decision may change, and this is already indicated by its low confidence. Order robustness is learned in every model we tested. Option isolation (Section C.2) is an attention mask that would make the pointer head robust to option order by construction, but it can only be applied to attention-only backbone models. The backbones of Drex v1.5, v2.0, and Max are hybrids with recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, which cannot apply such mask, so we have not tested option isolation on any of our released models.

sections.title: 8.6 Vision benchmarks
sections.content: On the 11 public vision benchmarks of the Decision Index (Table 21 in the Appendix), Drex Max has its highest accuracy on documents (InfographicVQA 98.8%, key-information extraction from receipts and forms 95.5%, and questions about charts in CharXiv 86.1%) and on selecting the correct element of web page for web agent (Mind2Web 88.6%). It has its lowest accuracy on benchmarks whose images require multi-step reasoning or cultural context: MMMU-Pro (53.6%), R-Bench-M (48.9%), and Hateful Memes (70.6%, which corresponds to chance-corrected skill of only 41.1, since Hateful Memes is binary task). We also compare Max with GPT-6 Luna Decisions on the same sample of 80 items from each benchmark for both models. Max is more accurate than Luna on all 11 benchmarks, and its normalized accuracy of the Decision Index vision leaderboard is 13.2 points higher (77.1 vs. 63.9), computed on this sample. On Decision Bench, Max answers 93.4% of the text-only questions and 98.3% of the 60 image-only questions correctly when it receives the images via its image encoder (Section 8.2). Together with the vision benchmarks, this suggests that the accuracy of Max on image inputs is close to its accuracy on text inputs for extraction and grounding, and lower for visual reasoning. However, these comparisons are made across different benchmarks, not between the same questions given once as images and once as text.

sections.title: 8.7 Evaluation of training checkpoints
sections.content: We evaluated seven checkpoints that were saved during the training of Drex v2.0 (Table 6 and Figure 9). We evaluated each checkpoint on all benchmarks of Decision Index 0.2.1, for which we report the chance-corrected skill score, overall and in each of its five domains, and on JevBench-231, for which we report accuracy. We also evaluated each checkpoint in game arena from OpenSpiel [31], where the model plays eight games against Jev 1.13.0, and it chooses each move by answering single choice question whose options are the set of legal moves. The score of model in the game arena is (wins + 1/2 draws)/games. We find that most of the improvement in the Decision Index skill score occurs in Stage 1: the score rises from 58.27 at step 3.6k to 60.02 at step 6.8k and then plateaus (60.01 at step 9.0k). Between steps 3.6k and 6.8k, the skill improves in the Knowledge domain (+2.6), the Arts domain (+4.1), and the Tools domain (+2.5). Stage 2, the specialization stage, raises the Decision Index skill score by 0.55 points by step 325, and by 0.64 points at its best checkpoint, at step 250. This improvement is almost entirely due to improvement in the Retrieval domain, in which the skill rises by 1.8 points by step 250. Stage 2 also gives the largest improvement in JevBench accuracy, from 84.0% to 87.0% at step 175, although the accuracy then decreases to 85.7% at step 250. sections.content: We compare variants of Drex Max that share the backbone, the training data, and the training schedule of the released model, but each of which differs from it in one training component  (Table 7)  : (1) model trained without RLAF, (2) model trained without the consistency terms in the loss function in both SFT and RLAF, and (3) model trained without the vision training stage. The models trained without RLAF and without the vision training stage are intermediate checkpoints that were saved during the training of the released model. The model trained without the consistency terms ℓπ and ℓs was trained separately, with SFT and then RLAF, from the same base model, with λπ = λs = 0 and otherwise with the hyperparameters listed in Table 11 in the Appendix. We evaluate each variant on all public requests of Decision Index 0.4.1 (Section 8.4) and on the 1,591 decisions of our study of option-order robustness (Section 8.5). Effect of RLAF. RLAF has the clearest effect. Relative to SFT alone, it adds 2.0 points to the Decision Index score and 1.5 percentage points of accuracy and lowers ECE by 0.9 percentage points. All three differences are statistically significant. Effect of the consistency loss terms. We find that the consistency terms in the loss function matter for the robustness of the model to the ordering of the options, but not for its accuracy. Without these terms, the model after RLAF reaches nearly the same Decision Index score (66.4 vs. 66.9, which is within the variation between repeated evaluations of the same model) and nearly the same accuracy as the model trained with these terms. However, its flip rate rises from 4.2% to 6.3% (about 67 vs. 100 of the 1,591 decisions). On the decisions with 6 options, the flip rate is also higher for the model trained without the consistency terms (from 13.0% to 17.8%), but this subset is too small for the difference to be statistically significant. The model trained without the consistency terms in either stage also has higher flip rate than the model trained with SFT alone with the terms (6.3% vs. 5.3%). This may be due to the judges preferences for specific orderings being distilled into the target model during RLAF. However, these two models differ in both training stages, so this comparison does not properly isolate the effect of RLAF. In addition, RLAF with the consistency terms lowers the flip rate by 1.1 percentage points relative to SFT alone (from 5.3% to 4.2%).

sections.title: 9 Deployment and inference optimization
sections.content: In this section, we discuss how the Drex models are served in production settings. Serving decision model is different problem than serving language model. Inference for language models is heavily focused on optimizing the decode loop. Decision models do not have decode loop. They read the request (a state plus one or more typed questions) in single prefill pass, and pointer head returns probability distribution over each questions options. The state is encoded once and shared by all questions. As result, the entire cost of request lands in one compute-heavy pass. That brings its own challenges: short requests are dominated by kernel-launch overhead, long states strain GPU memory, and the latency budget is tight because decision models usually sit in the request path of another system. The techniques in this section address these challenges.

sections.title: 9.1 Latency optimizations
sections.content: A decision model answers request in single forward pass, so the latency of request is the time that pass takes. This subsection first describes the two steps of the forward pass of pointer model and shows which step dominates the latency. It then describes three optimizations that reduce this latency: shared prefill, which processes the context once for all questions in request; CUDA Graphs, which remove the overhead of launching many small GPU kernels; and kernel changes, which make individual GPU kernels faster. Section 9.2 describes how we check that these optimizations do not lower accuracy. Two steps of the forward pass. The forward pass of pointer model on request can be divided into two steps. In the state pass, the model encodes the context, and the cost of this step grows with the length of the context. In the question pass, which runs once per question, the model processes only the tokens of that question, so this step is fast. We distinguish these two passes because question never attends to the tokens of another question, so the predicted probability depends only on the context and on the content of its own question. For given context, only the first question pays for the state pass. Every later question, whether in the same request or in later request that retrieves the encoded context from cache, costs much less because it skips the state pass. For example, once context of 114k to 117k tokens has been encoded and cached, each further question about it is answered in 21.6 ms, which is faster than the state pass on new context of only 2k tokens (35.6 ms). The state pass on new contexts therefore dominates the cost of inference: on fresh context of 131,072 tokens (the maximum), it takes about 2.7 s, above our 2 target for that worst case. Shared prefill. general-purpose inference engine treats each question as separate row, i.e., sequence that includes the full context, so request with many questions encodes its context once per question. sections.title: 9.2 Accuracy, latency, and cost
sections.content: When experimenting with inference optimizations, we classify each as exact (bit-identical outputs, e.g. parallel tokenization and CUDA Graphs over question rows), answer-changing (outputs may shift, e.g. FP8 and kernel fusion), or rejected (slower, or shifting outputs too much); Section lists each. To accept an answer-changing optimization, we check that it does not lower accuracy beyond threshold set for each model. We score the same questions with and without the change and compute 95% paired bootstrap interval on the accuracy difference. Most changes stayed within the threshold and changed few answers  (Table 9)  ; when one did not, we weighed the accuracy lost against the speed gained. The end-to-end inference stack, compared with the native-precision model, also stays within the threshold. Table 8 reports the median latency of single request and the cost per 1,000 decisions for the Drex models and the baselines.

sections.title: 10 Discussion and limitations
sections.content: Pointer and readout heads. The pointer head and the readout head suit different use-cases. The pointer head shares one encoding of the context across every question, which makes processing

sections.title: DREX TECHNICAL REPORT
sections.content: many questions over long documents cheap and makes the questions independent of each other by construction, up to floating-point error. The readout head encodes the context again for each question, with non-causal attention in its global attention layers (Section 5.2). Drex Max, which uses the readout head, is more accurate, especially on knowledge-intensive and multi-step decisions. Because Drex Max also differs from the pointer models in its attention mask, its dense 27B backbone, and its training data, isolating the contribution of each of these components is future work. One such study would compare two decision models that use the same Qwen3.8-27B backbone and the same training data: one with pointer head whose query and key projections are 256-dimensional (Section 4), and one with readout head, each trained with and without the non-causal attention mask. Closed-book knowledge. Every Drex model trails frontier chat models on evaluations that test closed-book knowledge, and the gap is largest on the hardest questions (HLE, GPQA). An output head can only rank options using the knowledge in the backbone model. single forward pass may also be poor substitute for long chain-of-thought reasoning and tool use. We have not tested this: such an experiment would let the model generate chain of thought, or call tools such as search engine, before its output head ranks the options, and would compare its accuracy on these benchmarks with that of the same model using single forward pass. The gap in performance narrows from v1.5 to v2.0 to Max. On the 37 benchmarks of the public subset of Decision Index 0.4.1, the skill score of the Drex models in the Knowledge domain, as reported on the leaderboard  (Table 1)  , rises from 44.6 for v1.5 to 47.9 for v2.0 and to 57.1 for Max. However, the gap remains non-zero in our largest model. Calibration and robustness to option order. Drex Max is slightly over-confident: in each of the four domains other than Language, its mean confidence exceeds its accuracy by 59 percentage points, and on questions with 6 to 20 options its ECE is 8.4% (Section 8.4). In addition, its deployed temperature (Tdep=1.009), which was fitted on held-out records from our training distribution, differs from the temperature that is fitted on held-out Decision Index decisions (Section 8.4). On questions with six or more options, 13% of its decisions have different most probable option when the order in which the options are listed in the request is randomly permuted (Section 8.5). Both effects concentrate on low-confidence decisions: the decisions whose most probable option changes when the options are reordered are largely the decisions to which the model assigns the lowest confidence (Table 20 in the Appendix). An application that uses the model can therefore reduce the impact of both effects by routing on confidence: it acts automatically only on decisions whose confidence (the probability of the most probable option) is above threshold, and sends the remaining decisions to human review or to different system. The threshold should be tuned on data from the setting in which the model is deployed, since the confidence of the model at given accuracy differs between domains and between numbers of options. Our study of option order uses 1,591 decisions and excludes requests whose options are structured objects rather than strings (Section L). larger study would give more precise estimates. study that also replaces the option codes of Drex Max (Section 5.2) with other tokens, for example 1, 2, 3 instead of A, B, C, would also show whether the model depends on the specific codes, in addition to the order of the options. Comparability. The systems on the Decision Index leaderboard  (Table 1)  differ from each other in several respects at the same time: the backbone model, the training data, the training objective, and the inference setup. Therefore, the difference between the scores of two systems in Table 1 should not be attributed to single design decision. Section discusses the scope of our evaluation, the latency of the models on long inputs and the accuracy checks of our inference code, and how applications should deploy and monitor decision model responsibly.

sections.title: 11 Conclusion
sections.content: For each input request, Drex outputs probability distribution over set of options that the user defines in the request. The three pointer models (Drex DLM, v1.5, and v2.0) are built on the open Kev code base. They encode the context of request once and share this encoding across all of its

sections.title: DREX TECHNICAL REPORT
sections.content: questions, they keep the answer to each question independent of the other questions, and they compute the probability of the options of each question with the pointer head (Section 4.1). The models are designed to produce outputs with very low latency. On Drex v1.5, new question about cached state of 114117k tokens is answered in 21.6 ms (Section 9). Drex Max uses dense multimodal backbone with 27B parameters, removes the causal attention mask in its full-attention layers, and encodes the context again for every question (Section 5). On Decision Index 0.4.1, it scores 67.52 on the public 37 benchmarks and 66.60 on the full score, which includes the private subset  (Table 1)  . On Decision Bench v4, with images provided to the model via its image encoder, its accuracy is 94.0%, which is not significantly different from that of GPT-6 Sol and d3-turbo, and 1.6 percentage points below that of Claude Opus 5.5 (Section 8.2). Its latency on Decision Bench is 0.66 s, compared with 2.1 for GPT-6 Sol and 4.3 for Claude Opus 5.5 (Section 9). Through our experiments, we are able to provide answers to the main research questions: RQ1 (calibration): The Drex models, which are trained with proper scoring rules, have an ECE of 1.44.5% at their deployed temperatures on the Decision Index decisions, which decreases to 0.8 1.4% after tuning the temperature on Decision Index examples (Section 8.4). However, the ECE within individual domains and on questions with many options is higher, so single temperature parameter is not substitute for monitoring calibration on each workload. RQ2 (option order): random permutation of the order of the options changes the most probable option in 4.35.9% of the decisions of each model, and changes accuracy by at most 1.2 percentage points (Section 8.5). On the workloads that we evaluated, the decisions that change are largely those to which the model already assigns low confidence. RQ3 (training): During the training of v2.0, most of the improvement in the Decision Index score was made in the first stage, SFT, and the later stages added smaller gains in specific domains (Section 8.7). For Max, adding RLAF after SFT raises the Decision Index score by 2.0 points, and the consistency terms in the loss function lower the flip rate from 6.3% to 4.2% while leaving the Decision Index score nearly unchanged  (Table 7)  . RQ4 (capacity, attention, and modality): Max differs from the pointer models in the size of its backbone, its attention mask, its output head, and its training data. It is more accurate than the pointer models, especially in the Knowledge domain of Decision Index. There are number of questions that remain open. All Drex models trail frontier chat models on evaluations that test closed-book knowledge. Further research might provide ways to mitigate this limitation, perhaps by routing knowledge-intensive queries to other systems. Additionally, architectural ablations, such as comparison of the pointer head and the readout head and of the causal and non-causal attention masks on the same backbone, are needed to show how much each component contributes to the gains of Max.

sections.title: A Extended related work
sections.content: Discriminative scoring. Scoring each candidate option by its likelihood under the language model is the standard way to evaluate language models on multiple-choice tasks [8, 24]. This score is biased by the length and exact wording of each option (for example, longer options tend to receive lower likelihood), and it requires separate forward pass for each option. In multiple-choice prompting, all options are presented in one prompt, each labeled with symbol (A, B, . . . ), and the model scores the symbol tokens instead of the option texts [61]. This removes the length bias and requires single forward pass for all options, but it works only if the model correctly associates each symbol with the option that it labels. The readout head of Drex Max (Section 5) is trained version of this approach: bias-free linear layer maps the final hidden state to one logit per option code. Cross-encoders [13, 46] score each (query, candidate) pair with classification head, so they require one forward pass per candidate, and their cost grows linearly with the number of candidates. Pointer networks [71] output probability distribution over the positions of their input, and therefore over set of candidates whose size can differ from one input to the next. The Drex pointer models combine these two ideas. As in cross-encoder, the options are placed in the input together with the question, delimited by special tokens that user text cannot produce (Section C.1). As in pointer network, pointer head then selects among the options, using single forward pass over the state and the question. Option-order sensitivity. Language models answering multiple-choice questions favor particular option positions or symbols, so permuting the options changes their answers [53, 85]. Averaging the predictions over permutations of the options reduces this bias, but it multiplies the inference cost by the number of permutations. The options of decision model are often actions that an application will take, so its predicted distribution should not depend on the arbitrary order in which the developer lists them. For decision model, sensitivity to option order is therefore an error of the model rather than an artifact of the benchmark. Option isolation, an attention mask under which each option attends only to the state, the instruction, and itself, makes the pointer head permutation-equivariant by construction (Section C.2). It cannot be applied to the hybrid backbones of Drex v1.5, v2.0, and Max, since their recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers cannot apply an arbitrary attention mask. Section 8.5 measures how robust to option order these models become through training alone. Calibration and proper scoring. Modern neural networks are often over-confident [23]. Temperature scaling, which divides the logits by single constant fitted on held-out data, is simple and effective fix that is applied after training, and it does not change the ranking of the options [23]. After pre-training, the token probabilities of language models are reasonably well calibrated on multiple-choice questions [28, 29]. Confidences that model states in text (verbalized confidences)

The Drex decision heads can be attached to backbones of different architectures, and the family uses three kinds  (Table 12)  : Drex DLM uses an autoregressive-to-diffusion conversion with block-bidirectional attention [19], which is related to masked diffusion language models [45, 62]; Drex v1.5 and Drex Max use hybrids of Gated DeltaNet linear-attention layers and full-attention layers [56, 79, 83]; Drex v2.0 uses hybrid of the same kind whose feed-forward blocks are sparse mixtures of experts [18, 55, 64]. Decision Index [37] aggregates decision benchmarks from several domains: knowledge and reasoning (e.g., MMLU-Pro, GPQA, and BBH [60, 68, 74]), language, retrieval, tool use, and arts. It reports the score on each benchmark as skill that is corrected for chance, so that 0 corresponds to uniform guessing (Section 7). Decision Bench [4] samples decision questions with fixed set of options from 36 public datasets of real-world records, such as receipts, documents, and photographs.

The five delimiter tokens (<state>, <q>, <opt>, </opt>, and <decide>) are rarely used special tokens that already exist in the Qwen vocabulary (<fim_prefix>, <fim_middle>, <box_start>, <box_end>, and <fim_suffix>), so no new rows have to be added to the embedding matrix. Before tokenization, user text is rewritten so that it cannot produce these tokens. User text therefore cannot imitate delimiter, and the boundaries between options are always those defined by the request. Each token carries three ids. The segment id seg(i) is 0 for the tokens of the state and for the tokens of question block bk. The position ids of every question block start immediately after the state, so question block has the same position ids regardless of how many questions precede it. The option index identifies the option that the token belongs to. C.2 Segment-masked attention On backbones that consist only of attention layers, the packed sequence of Eq. (16) is encoded under the block-causal mask, under which token may attend to token (Mij = 1) only if does not come after and belongs either to the state or to the same segment as i: Mij = 1 (cid:0)seg(j) = 0 seg(j) = seg(i)(cid:1), (17) This mask is shown in Figure 10a. Under this mask, the state never attends to question, and no question attends to another question. The pointer models use two variants of this scheme, described in the next two paragraphs. Bidirectional state (Drex DLM). Efficient-DLM is trained with bidirectional attention inside blocks [19], so Drex DLM enables the state_bidir option, which additionally sets Mij = 1 whenever both tokens belong to the state, i.e., seg(i) = seg(j) = 0 (Figure 10b). Every token of the state then attends to every other token of the state. The state still never attends to question block, so the cached keys and values of the state do not depend on the questions and can be reused exactly for every question. Row-wise form (Drex v1.5, v2.0). Gated DeltaNet layers [83] process the sequence with recurrent state that summarizes all previous tokens, so they cannot apply an arbitrary attention mask. On hybrid backbones, each question is therefore processed as its own causal sequence [S; bk], which we call row. Each row starts from the cached result of processing the state S, i.e., the keyvalue cache of the full-attention layers and the recurrent state of the DeltaNet layers. Each row contains exactly the tokens that Eq. (17) allows question to attend to, at the same position ids. On attention-only backbones, the packed form and the row form therefore produce the same outputs up to floating-point error.

On attention-only backbones, the mask can additionally restrict each option span (the tokens from <opt> to </opt>) to attend only to the state, the instruction of its question, and itself (Figure 10c). The <decide> token still attends to every option span, and all option spans of question start at the same position id. Under this mask, the hidden states of an option do not depend on the other options or on their order, so reordering the options reorders the probabilities of the pointer head in the same way: the pointer head is permutation-equivariant by construction. Hybrid backbones cannot apply this mask, so they must learn robustness to option order from the training data instead (Section 6.2). Section 8.5 measures how robust to option order they become. Remark 1 (Question independence). Under Eq. (17) (or its bidirectional-state or row variants), with position ids of the question block restarting after the state, the output distribution pk of question depends only on the state and question block bk, since every attention or recurrent path into segment passes only through segments 0 and k. Adding, removing, or reordering other questions therefore leaves pk unchanged up to floating-point error. Drex Max satisfies the same property trivially, since each question is encoded as its own sequence (Section 5). This property follows directly from the mask. It ensures that batched inference, replaying subset of the questions of request (e.g., for an audit), and caching individual questions produce the same outputs, up to floating-point error, as processing the full request. The property assumes that every feed-forward or MoE layer processes each token independently of the other tokens. This holds at inference for dense, hybrid, and MoE backbones, since MoE routing at inference does not drop tokens when an expert exceeds its capacity.

sections.title: E Model family
sections.content: Drex DLM. The backbone is NVIDIA Efficient-DLM-8B [19], an autoregressive language model that was converted into diffusion language model. It splits the sequence into blocks of consecutive tokens, with causal attention across blocks and bidirectional attention within each block, and it is trained with position-dependent masking. We attach the pointer head, enable bidirectional attention within the state (state_bidir, Section C.2), and fine-tune both the head and the backbone [39]. Since its backbone consists only of attention layers, all questions of request are processed in single forward pass over the packed sequence (Section C.1). It is released under CC BY-NC 4.0 [11], the license of its backbone. Drex v1.5. Drex v1.5 is the smallest model of the family whose weights are released under license that permits commercial use (Open RAIL-M [43]) [38]. Its backbone, MiMo-V2.6-Distill-Qwen-9B, is 32-layer Qwen3.5 hybrid with 8.95B parameters and three Gated DeltaNet layers for each full-attention layer. Xiaomi MiMo trained it by distillation [7880, 82]. Drex v2.0. Drex v2.0 is larger successor of v1.5, and its weights are also openly released [42]. Its backbone is the language model of Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, vision-language mixture-of-experts model [55, 82]. We discard the image encoder and the output layer that predicts the next token (the LM head). It has 40 layers with the same 3:1 DeltaNet/full-attention pattern as v1.5 and MoE feed-forward blocks that route each token to 8 of 256 experts, so about 3B of 35B parameters are active per token. Drex Max. Drex Max is the largest member of the family and the only one that accepts images as input (Section 5) [40]. It differs from the other models in three ways: it uses readout head instead of pointer head, it removes the causal mask in its full-attention layers, and it processes each question as separate sequence, so the state is not cached and shared across questions (Section D.1). Its request and output formats are the same as those of the other models, so request written for v1.5 is also valid for Max.

sections.title: G Evaluation details
sections.content: Decision Index versions. Version 0.2.1 contains 38 benchmarks across five domains: Knowledge (10), Language (10), Retrieval (6), Tools (5), and Arts (7). Each domain is weighted in proportion to the square root of its number of benchmarks, except Arts, whose weight is fixed at 10%. Version 0.4.1 removes ForecastBench, rebuilds GSM8K, and moves WinoGrande to different domain. Its public index averages 37 benchmarks with fixed domain weights: Knowledge 25.8%, Language 25.8%, Retrieval 20.0%, Tools 18.3%, and Arts 10%. These weights are rounded to one decimal, so the printed values sum to 99.9% although the weights sum to 100%. Its Full score adds private items, run by the maintainers of the leaderboard, that test either the same skills as the public benchmarks or new domains. Where model has both published public-index score (reported on the 0.4.1 leaderboard) and our rerun of the public suite, the two differ by at most 0.1 point on the Decision Index (61.25 vs. 61.24 for v2.0, 58.08 vs. 57.98 for v1.5), consistent with the variation between repeated evaluations of the same model. Other evaluations. sections.title: I Further limitations and broader impact
sections.content: Confounds and evaluation scope. The systems on the Decision Index leaderboard differ in backbone, training data, training objective, and inference setup at the same time. Differences between the rows of Table 1 and the per-benchmark changes in Figure 11 should therefore not be attributed to any single factor. The full scores are taken from the leaderboard. We did not run the private tests ourselves, and we do not have the outputs of the models on individual private test items. JevBench no longer separates the strongest decision models from each other (Section H.3). Decision Bench contains only 60 questions whose state consists of an image alone, which is small sample for conclusions about image inputs, so our claims about images rest mainly on the vision suites (Section 8.6). Benchmarks drawn from public datasets may overlap with the pre-training data of the teacher models despite our filters (Section F.1). Inference efficiency. On Drex v1.5, request with an uncached state at the maximum length of 131,072 tokens takes about 2.7 s, which exceeds our target of 2 s. The cost of Drex Max on long state grows with the number of questions, since it processes the state once per question (Section D.1). We check the accuracy after each change to the inference code separately.  (Table 9)  . Output probabilities can differ slightly when the same request is processed in batch with different other requests, because the low-precision kernels choose their tiling by batch shape. Broader impact and responsible use. decision model is designed so that an application can act on its output automatically, without human in the loop. By construction, it can only return one of the options that the user supplied. Its calibration and its robustness to option order, in contrast, are empirical properties: we measure them on benchmark data, and they can degrade when the inputs differ from that data. Image inputs give attackers additional ways to inject adversarial content, since the model also processes text that is rendered inside an image. Users should therefore treat state that contains images as untrusted input, just as they would state that contains text. The probabilities are reproducible only up to the numerical variation reported in Section 9. decision whose probability is close to its threshold can therefore change between runs, and decision with many options can change when the options are reordered. Deployments should monitor confidence and accuracy on live traffic. They should also keep margin around decision thresholds, send low-confidence decisions to human review, and log the request, the output distribution, and the model version as the record of each decision. The model should not be the sole basis for consequential decisions about people. sections.content: L Order-robustness protocol Sampling. From the 37 benchmarks of the public index of Decision Index 0.4.1, we kept the requests in which every question is choice question and at least one gold label is string. Of these, we kept only the requests with at most 16 questions and state of at most 12,000 characters when serialized as JSON. Within each benchmark, we shuffled the requests with the benchmark id as the seed and kept the first 40 (or all of them, if benchmark has fewer), which gives 1,175 requests. Variants. For every question with at least two options, we built two variants: one with the options in reverse order and one with random permutation of the options, seeded by the request id and the question key. The instruction, the state, and the option texts are unchanged, and only the order of the options in the criteria field of the request changes. Requests. On 26 October 2026, we sent each variant of each request to drex-max, drex-v2.0, and drex-v1.5 at drex.nace.ai and to jev-1.14.0 at api.typesafe.ai, with up to eight concurrent requests per model. Each model answered each variant once: request that failed with transient error was resent, with increasing delays, until it received an answer. Exclusions. The public APIs reject requests whose options are structured objects rather than strings (e.g., chord or preference options with several fields), since such requests fail their schema validation (HTTP 422). The evaluation code of the Decision Index converts such options into strings before sending them, but we sent the requests unchanged, so these requests are excluded. Jev also rejected some requests, which we excluded as well. Any request not answered in all three orders by all four models is excluded for every model, leaving 1,040 requests and 1,591 decisions. Scoring. We renormalize the predicted probabilities over the supplied options, map them back to the original order of the options, and compare them as in Section 3. Bootstrap intervals are computed by resampling decisions, with 2,000 resamples.

sections.content: In this section, we present an application of Drex Max within our enterprise document search framework, which answers natural-language questions over workspace of customers documents, spreadsheets, and tables. To answer search query, the framework must decide which search strategy to use, which files to access, and whether the text it has already retrieved is enough to answer the query without accessing more files. Drex Max makes these decisions, and separate language model, which we call the answering model, writes the final answer from the content that the framework selects. Each decision is single noul question (Section 3): Drex Max returns the probability that the answer is yes, and the framework compares this probability with threshold that we fitted for that type of decision. File relevance decides which of the retrieved files are most likely to contain the information that the query asks for. Table relevance decides which of the retrieved tables the framework can skip. Passage sufficiency decides whether the passages already retrieved from file contain the complete answer. Table 26 summarizes the four types. Routing search queries. The framework therefore removes table from the shortlist when Drexs probability for it is below fitted threshold, unless the table has the highest probability on the shortlist. We fitted this threshold on 4,826 screening decisions, each of which is pair of query and one file on its shortlist, from searches over two evaluation workspaces in which every query is annotated with the files that contain its answer. On these decisions, this simple thresholding approach correctly retains 99.1% of the files that contain the gold answer and removes 12% of the files that do not. Checking whether retrieved passages already answer the query. For each shortlisted file, the retrieval system also returns its passages, which are the text chunks of that file that matched the query, and its graph facts, which are short statements about entities in the file, such as the due date of an invoice, that the framework extracted from the file when indexing it. Normally, fact search then fetches the content of each shortlisted file and passes it to the answering model. Before doing so, the framework asks Drex, separately for each file, whether these passages and graph facts alone contain every required component of the answer, for the entity, period, and document that the query names. If the probability is above high threshold for any file, the framework does not fetch the content of any file, and the answering model writes the answer from the passages of the files that passed this check, citing those files. The threshold is high because the framework does not check such an answer against the files afterwards. We fitted it on 103 recorded searches with reference answers, for each of which we graded both the answer written from passages and the answer written from the fetched files against the reference. At this threshold, 37 of the 103 searches are answered from passages, and for none of them the answer from passages was graded worse than the answer from the fetched files. When we reran these searches, no probability changed by more than 0.005, so the decisions are reproducible. Fitting the thresholds. We fit each threshold in the labeled examples of its decision type described above. Thresholds are specific to the model: when fitted in the same way, the routing threshold is 0.80 for Drex Max, 0.51 for v2.0, and 0.25 for v1.5, and with Maxs threshold, v2.0 would route 6 percentage points fewer queries correctly. In accordance with Section 8.4, threshold must therefore be changed whenever the model changes.

Each technique is described once, under the first model that used it. N.1 Inference efficiency of Drex v1.5 Unless stated otherwise, the measurements in this subsection are median latencies of the released Drex v1.5 checkpoint on one NVIDIA B200 GPU, measured in September 2026. They exclude the time spent in the API gateway, which receives requests and forwards them to the model. Execution model. Section 9.1 describes the two passes of request to pointer model: the state pass, which processes the state once and whose cost grows with the length of the state, and the question pass, which runs once per question and processes only the tokens of that question. For Drex v1.5, new question about cached state of 114117k tokens is answered in 21.6 ms, which is faster than processing an uncached state of 2k tokens (35.6 ms; Figure 13a). Processing an uncached state remains the main cost: it takes 1.78 for state of 114117k tokens and about 2.7 at the maximum length of 131,072 tokens, almost all of it in the state pass (Figure 13b). The latter exceeds our target of 2 for this worst case. Optimizations. We run Drex v1.5 on inference code that we wrote for the pointer models, rather than on general-purpose inference engine such as vLLM [30]. We batch requests with short states, since the time needed to launch GPU kernels dominates their latency. We do not batch requests with long states: their computation already saturates the GPU, and batching them doubled the median latency without increasing throughput. The optimizations are standard techniques, so we list them without their tuning parameters. Our inference code uses FP8 matrix multiplications in the linear projections, using custom kernel that is compared bit for bit with the PyTorch matrix multiplication when the inference server starts, and that falls back to the PyTorch kernel for every shape where the two differ. CUDA graphs, which record sequence of GPU kernels once and replay it with single launch, captured for the input shapes that occur in real requests. Variable-length FlashAttention [12]. An attention kernel in which the rows of all questions (Section C.2) use single copy of the cached keys and values of the state, instead of one copy per row. Kernels that take the sequence length as an argument at runtime, instead of being compiled separately for each length. Nearly every request with long state has length that has not occurred before, so kernels compiled for each length would have to be compiled while the request waits. Parallel tokenization of long states, with output identical to sequential tokenization. Skipping the attention output and the feed-forward computation of the last layer for state tokens, since the pointer head uses only the hidden states at the <decide> and </opt> tokens. Compared with the previous version of our inference code, these optimizations together reduced the latency of new question about cached state of 114117k tokens from 254 ms to 21.6 ms, and the latency of request with an uncached state of the same length from 2.22 to 1.78 s. Passing the sequence length at runtime reduced the latency of the first request at new length from over second, most of which was spent compiling kernels, to about 160 ms. Parallel tokenization reduced the tokenization time of the longest states from 0.3 to 0.1 s. Skipping the unused computation in the last layer reduced latency by 5% at the maximum length of 131,072 tokens and left all 1,200 outputs that we checked unchanged. All of these gains are measured relative to our earlier inference code, not relative to another inference engine. N.2 Inference efficiency of Drex v2.0 Unlike v1.5, Drex v2.0 is served with general-purpose inference engine, which processes each question as separate sequence that contains the full state. Shared prefill. Without further changes, request with many questions would therefore process its state once per question. Shared prefill processes the prefix that all questions of request have in common only once, and each question then processes only the rest of its sequence. We apply it only to requests with more than one question and state of at least 1,024 tokens. For shorter states, sharing was slower than processing each question separately and changed the output probabilities slightly. For states of 8k tokens with 16 questions and 8 concurrent clients, shared prefill increased throughput tenfold. The speedup per request grew with the length of the state, from 68 times at 8k tokens to 1112 times at 32k tokens, and for states of at least 1,024 tokens the outputs were bit-identical to those without sharing. Negative results. FlashAttention-4 was slower than the previous attention kernel on short inputs, so v2.0 uses it only for inputs of at least 8,192 tokens. Quantization to FP8 at runtime (online), to MXFP8, or to NVFP4 gave at most 1.1 speedup and changed the accuracy, so v2.0 uses none of them. N.3 Inference efficiency of Drex Max Drex Max cannot share the processed state between questions (Section D.1), so every question requires processing the full state. Our inference work on Drex Max therefore focuses on the speed of individual kernels on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs (B200 and B300). Every change that alters the output probabilities was checked against the accuracy criterion for Drex Max (Section 9.2). Recurrent layers. The Gated DeltaNet layers of Drex Max originally ran on kernels that we wrote in Triton. Replacing them with the prefill kernel of FlashInfer for Blackwell GPUs reduced latency by 916% for states of 8k to 128k tokens. On the 11,096 decisions of our accuracy panel (Section 9.2), accuracy changed by 0.13 points, and 98.7% of the top options agreed with those of the same model with the previous kernels, which is within the criterion for Drex Max. We consider this kernel an interim solution. MLP quantization. Quantizing all 128 MLP projections to NVFP4, instead of 96 of them, reduced the median latency by about 8%. The mean accuracy on our panel was essentially unchanged relative to FP8 (87.42 and 87.53). On the When2Call panel, however, accuracy was 2.00 points higher than with BF16 reference (95% interval +0.60 to +3.40), which exceeds our limit of 1.5 points per dataset (Section 9.2). We nevertheless released the change after manual review, and we report the difference here. Hardware. With single client, Drex Max ran 1732% faster on B300 GPU than on B200 for states of 4k tokens or more. With 16 concurrent clients and states of 32k tokens, this advantage fell to 3%. On B300, accuracy on When2Call was 1.04 points below the BF16 reference on B200, which is within the limit of 1.5 points per dataset.
